We Built Software Security for Humans. AI Agents May Force Us to Rethink Everything.  My theory is simple: the software security architecture we rely on evolved around human-scale threats. Artificial intelligence is changing that equation, and I believe we may need what I call Software Security V2.  I've been developing software since 2010.  For more than 16 years, software engineering has been one of the central priorities of my life. I've worked with frontend technologies, backend systems, databases, APIs, authentication, cloud infrastructure and many of the technologies that make modern applications possible.  I've built software for hundreds of clients and spent years developing my own SaaS platform, SelfManager[.]ai.  I'm not a cybersecurity specialist, and I don't claim to be.  But I've spent enough time building and maintaining complex software to understand how many things must work together correctly, how easily unexpected behavior can emerge, and how difficult securing interconnected systems can become.  And lately, something has been concerning me.  I believe we're approaching a point where the architecture and security practices we've relied on for decades may no longer be sufficient for the capabilities of increasingly advanced AI agents.  I have a personal theory about this.  Software Security V1 was built around human-scale threats. Software Security V2 will need to defend against machine-scale threats.  And after watching Sam Altman's recent interview at Stanford, I believe the underlying concern deserves much more attention.  My Theory: What I Mean by Software Security V1  Let me explain.  Modern software infrastructure wasn't designed overnight.  It evolved over decades, with programming languages, operating systems, databases, networks, frameworks and security practices becoming increasingly sophisticated.  Throughout that evolution, human capabilities shaped how software was developed, tested, maintained and attacked.  A highly skilled security researcher might spend weeks or months investigating a complex application.  Discovering an unusual vulnerability could require exceptional technical knowledge, extensive experimentation and a deep understanding of how different components interact.  Of course, automated vulnerability scanners, fuzzers, botnets and sophisticated exploitation tools existed long before modern AI.  Human researchers have discovered extremely serious vulnerabilities for decades.  So when I say Security V1 was built around human-scale threats, I'm not suggesting earlier software was impossible to compromise or that every vulnerability required a human to discover it manually.  I'm saying that human expertise, time, resources and the capabilities of available tools helped determine the practical limits of vulnerability discovery.  Consider a software system containing millions of lines of code and hundreds of dependencies.  Some of those dependencies may themselves contain millions of additional lines of code.  A vulnerability could exist in a component for years without anyone identifying it.  Not necessarily because it was impossible to discover.  But because nobody had the necessary combination of expertise, motivation, time and resources to investigate that particular weakness.  I believe AI is beginning to change those constraints.  And that's where things become interesting.  AI Agents Are Changing the Economics of Finding Vulnerabilities  Imagine one person working with multiple sophisticated AI agents.  One agent investigates a programming language's source code.  Another examines how its components interact.  Another studies dependencies.  Another tests unexpected behavior.  And others attempt to reproduce findings, identify combinations of weaknesses or examine possible security consequences.  Now imagine those systems working continuously and sharing their discoveries.  This is no longer simply about a chatbot answering programming questions.  It's about increasingly autonomous systems that can use tools, execute code, coordinate investigations and work across different technical disciplines.  One person supported by sufficiently capable AI agents may eventually perform work that previously required an entire team of highly specialized researchers.  That doesn't mean AI will discover every vulnerability or that every finding will be exploitable.  These models still have limitations. They can make mistakes, misunderstand code, produce false positives and fail at complex investigations.  But their capabilities are improving.  And the potential consequences are substantial.  Previously impractical investigations could become economically affordable.  A task requiring weeks of human effort might eventually require hours or days of automated work.  And unlike a human researcher, an AI system can potentially scale an investigation across large amounts of computing resources.  I see enormous positive potential here.  These capabilities can help defenders secure systems that were previously too expensive or complicated to investigate thoroughly.  But there's another side.  The same capabilities could also help malicious actors discover weaknesses faster than organizations can fix them.  That is the central problem behind my theory.  Sam Altman's Warning Reinforces My Concern  On October 21, 2026, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman spoke at Stanford Graduate School of Business.  During the interview, he discussed the cybersecurity challenges created by increasingly capable AI models.  One particular statement caught my attention:  "I no longer think we're going to be able to just patch all the bugs."  Altman argued that as models become more capable, they could identify vulnerabilities that fall outside conventional threat models, potentially including weaknesses deep within software and hardware systems.  His broader point was that organizations may be underestimating how quickly these capabilities are developing.  And instead of relying entirely on fixing individual vulnerabilities as they're discovered, he suggested that cybersecurity may need a fundamentally different defensive model, potentially using advanced AI itself.  Watch Sam Altman's Stanford interview — cybersecurity discussion begins around 19 minutes  I found that particularly significant.  Because I've been thinking about a closely related problem, although from a somewhat different perspective.  Altman is questioning whether our existing approach to defending software can keep up.  I'm questioning whether the architectural assumptions underlying modern software security need to evolve as well.  These aren't identical arguments.  And Altman's warning doesn't prove my theory.  But it reinforces the importance of asking whether security processes designed around comparatively slower discovery and response cycles can withstand increasingly capable automated adversaries.  What happens when finding vulnerabilities becomes significantly faster than evaluating, fixing, testing and deploying the necessary security updates?  That's the question I believe the industry needs to confront.  October 2026 Is Already Providing Evidence  This isn't purely a discussion about what might become possible five or ten years from now.  Look at what happened during the week of October 19–23, 2026.  PHP: Two critical vulnerabilities were disclosed, each rated 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. Under vulnerable conditions, exploitation could allow unauthorized code execution or exposure of sensitive memory. OpenAI documented how AI-assisted research contributed to discovering one of these vulnerabilities.  Node.js: Security releases addressed several high-severity vulnerabilities, including a memory-corruption flaw that could potentially permit remote code execution. The Node.js project credited OpenAI Codex Security with discovering that issue.  Ruby and GitLab: Ruby released updates fixing flaws in its regular-expression engine that had contributed to serious vulnerabilities in GitLab, including an issue previously rated 10 out of 10.  Java and certificate infrastructure: A compromised certificate-authority incident required security responses across major software ecosystems, including an Oracle Java security update.  Python software ecosystem: Attackers compromised LiteLLM's release pipeline, distributing a malicious package designed to steal credentials and enable unauthorized code execution.  These are different types of security incidents.  Not all were discovered by AI. Not all were successful attacks. And the existence of a vulnerability does not mean every system using the affected technology was compromised.  But consider the technologies involved.  PHP and Node.js are used extensively to power internet applications.  Java is deeply integrated into enterprise computing.  Ruby underpins important software platforms.  Python packages are used throughout automation and AI development.  And digital certificates help establish trust between systems communicating over the internet.  We're discussing vulnerabilities and compromises affecting technologies that form part of the foundations of modern computing.  What surprises me, even after 16 years of working in software, is how deep some of the AI-assisted discoveries are reaching.  And my concern isn't limited to the vulnerabilities that have already been disclosed.  It's about what happens as these discovery capabilities improve.  AI Is Already Testing the Security Boundaries of AI Itself  On October 23, OpenAI published technical details about how it has strengthened security around its frontier-model training infrastructure.  In authorized internal research, fleets of advanced AI agents were instructed to investigate the infrastructure and test whether they could cross security boundaries.  According to OpenAI, those experiments uncovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities and configuration weaknesses.  The agents demonstrated ways to escape virtual-machine isolation, move across security boundaries and reach restricted network resources under certain experimental conditions.  The company subsequently strengthened its infrastructure, repaired vulnerabilities and expanded its defensive testing.  This doesn't mean an ordinary person can instruct any current AI model to compromise any computer.  These were specialized experiments performed under controlled conditions with substantial resources.  But they demonstrate something important.  Advanced AI agents are already capable of discovering unexpected weaknesses in complex security environments.  And this strengthens the case for examining whether our defensive assumptions need to change.  Read OpenAI's technical report: Securing Our Frontier Model Training Environment  Why I Believe Security V2 May Become Necessary  For me, the most important question isn't whether AI will discover more vulnerabilities.  I believe it will.  The harder question is what kind of software architecture can remain secure when increasingly powerful automated systems are constantly looking for weaknesses.  Historically, many security strategies have relied on identifying vulnerabilities, deploying patches, monitoring suspicious activity and preventing unauthorized access.  These practices remain essential.  I'm not suggesting that patching software will become unnecessary.  But what happens when the pace of discovering vulnerabilities increases dramatically?  What happens when attackers don't just target one application, but systematically investigate its programming language, dependencies, authentication systems, deployment infrastructure and cloud services?  And what happens when several seemingly minor weaknesses can be discovered and combined automatically?  I suspect we may need an architectural approach that assumes vulnerabilities will eventually be found, rather than relying primarily on preventing their discovery.  Some of the principles already exist.  We have isolation, sandboxing, least-privilege permissions, zero-trust architecture, defense in depth and many other established security practices.  But I believe the way we apply these principles may need to become substantially more rigorous.  For example:  A vulnerability in one component should not automatically provide access to unrelated systems.  A compromised application should have extremely limited access to credentials, infrastructure and sensitive information. AI agents should operate within enforceable permissions and security boundaries, not merely instructions telling them what they're allowed to do. Security analysis may need to become continuous, with defensive AI agents inspecting systems as frequently as attackers might. Organizations may need the ability to detect, verify and deploy security updates far more quickly than traditional engineering workflows allow. None of these ideas is entirely new.  But their importance changes when sophisticated vulnerability discovery becomes increasingly automated.  Security V2, as I imagine it, is not one new programming language or operating system.  It's a broader evolution toward software systems that can remain resilient even when powerful adversaries are capable of discovering and exploiting weaknesses at unprecedented speed.  And importantly, AI itself may become one of the most effective tools for building those defenses.  The Other Concern: Powerful AI May Become Accessible to More People  There's another aspect of this that I believe deserves attention.  The risk is not limited to the capabilities of the most advanced models today.  We also need to consider what happens when increasingly capable systems become widely accessible.  Some commercial AI systems include safeguards, monitoring and restrictions intended to reduce misuse.  But open-weight models can sometimes be modified and operated on infrastructure outside the original developer's control.  These models provide substantial benefits for innovation, research and competition.  However, their safeguards may also be more difficult to enforce once the models are distributed.  This does not establish that open-weight AI caused the security incidents discussed here.  Nor does it mean every open model is capable of sophisticated vulnerability discovery.  The concern is what becomes possible as the technology advances.  We don't necessarily need dramatically more intelligent models for the security landscape to change. We may also see major changes as people learn to combine existing models with increasingly powerful tools and coordinated agent systems.  Capabilities that once required significant resources could become more accessible.  And some people will inevitably attempt to use those capabilities maliciously.  This is one reason I believe the architecture itself needs to become more resilient.  Why the Next 30 Days Concern Me  On October 22, Anthropic's deputy Chief Information Security Officer, Jason D. Clinton, warned that cybersecurity conditions could become significantly worse before improving.  He suggested organizations might face approximately 18 months of difficult security challenges.  Marc Benioff, Salesforce's CEO, publicly supported the warning.  I agree with the broader concern.  But I'm looking at a shorter timeframe.  I believe the next 30 days, from October 23 to November 22, 2026, could be extremely challenging for the software security industry.  I expect more significant vulnerability disclosures, emergency security updates and attempts to exploit newly revealed weaknesses.  I also suspect we're going to learn more about security vulnerabilities that existed for years without being publicly identified.  That's my prediction, not an established forecast.  And I genuinely hope I'm wrong about the severity.  I'm not predicting that the internet will collapse or that critical services will necessarily fail.  But the amount of security work potentially ahead of us is considerable.  Especially when we remember that publicly disclosed vulnerabilities are only the ones we know about.  There may be other weaknesses that haven't yet been discovered or reported.  Some attackers may already possess information about vulnerabilities defenders don't know exist.  That's always been a possibility in cybersecurity.  AI could make that challenge considerably more difficult.  Software Engineers and Security Specialists May Be Needed More Than Ever  There's something else I find interesting about this situation.  We're constantly discussing how AI may replace software engineers.  But consider what happens if advanced AI substantially accelerates vulnerability discovery.  Someone still needs to understand the infrastructure.  Someone needs to determine whether an application is exposed.  Someone needs to develop or validate fixes.  Someone needs to understand the consequences of updating a dependency in a complex production environment.  And someone needs to ensure that the proposed solution doesn't introduce additional problems.  AI can already assist with many of these tasks and may increasingly automate portions of them.  But production software exists within real businesses, with real dependencies, customers, data and operational consequences.  Finding a vulnerability and safely fixing it across millions of deployed systems are two very different challenges.  In the near term, I suspect experienced software engineers, cybersecurity professionals and infrastructure specialists may face an exceptionally busy period.  And I believe strong engineering judgment will remain important, even as AI changes how much of the work is performed.  I Hope Our Software Infrastructure Holds Up  I want to end with something important.  I'm extremely optimistic about artificial intelligence.  I use AI extensively in software development, and I believe its potential benefits are extraordinary.  But optimism doesn't mean ignoring the risks.  And after watching what happened this week, I genuinely hope that technology companies, security researchers and engineering teams can respond quickly enough.  Because we're not just talking about small websites or isolated databases.  We're talking about infrastructure that supports banking, financial transactions, healthcare, communications, businesses, government services and everyday technologies most people never think about.  People simply expect these systems to work.  And they should be able to.  I hope security researchers continue finding critical vulnerabilities before malicious actors exploit them.  I hope AI becomes an extraordinary advantage for defenders.  And I hope the next 30 days prove my concerns too pessimistic.  But long term, I believe we need to take the architectural question seriously.  For decades, software security evolved around a world where human capabilities helped determine the limits of sophisticated attacks.  We're entering a world where increasingly capable AI agents may fundamentally change those limits.  My theory is that the software industry will eventually need to evolve from what I call Security V1 to Security V2.  Not because everything we built previously was wrong.  But because the threat environment may be changing faster than the systems designed to protect us.  Sam Altman's warning reinforces that concern.  And the developments of October 2026 suggest the transition is no longer a purely theoretical discussion.  Security V1 was shaped by human-scale threats.  Security V2 must be ready for machine-scale threats.  I hope we get there before serious damage forces us to.  Marian Sorca is a software engineer and founder of abZ Global and SelfManager[.]ai. He has worked in software development since 2010, delivering custom websites, business applications and SaaS platforms for clients, primarily in the United States. His technical experience includes frontend and backend engineering, cloud infrastructure, application architecture and AI integrations.

Major government investigations—including Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation and the Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee’s bipartisan counterintelligence report—documented over 100 contacts between Trump campaign associates and Russian-aligned individuals during the 2016 presidential election cycle.  1. Key Personnel & Their Russian Contacts Paul Manafort (Campaign Chairman) Contact: Shared internal campaign strategy and polling data with Konstantin Kilimnik, whom the Senate Intelligence Committee formally identified as a Russian intelligence officer. Details: The Senate panel concluded that Manafort’s proximity to Trump and willingness to share internal campaign data constituted a "grave counterintelligence threat".  Donald Trump Jr. & Jared Kushner Contact: The June 2016 Trump Tower Meeting with Russian attorney Natalia Veselnitskaya, music promoter Rob Goldstone, and former Soviet intelligence officer Rinat Akhmetshin. Details: Arranged after Goldstone promised "official documents and information that would incriminate Hillary" as "part of Russia and its government's support for Mr. Trump." Trump Jr. famously replied, "If it's what you say I love it."  George Papadopoulos (Foreign Policy Advisor) Contact: Communicated with Joseph Mifsud, a Maltese professor with links to Russian government officials, and Russian national Olga Vinogradova. Details: In April 2016, Mifsud informed Papadopoulos that the Russians possessed "dirt" on Hillary Clinton in the form of "thousands of emails." Papadopoulos later shared this information with an Australian diplomat, which triggered the FBI's initial "Crossfire Hurricane" counterintelligence probe.  Michael Flynn (National Security Advisor) Contact: Held secret communications with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak during the presidential transition period. Details: Discussed U.S. sanctions imposed on Russia by the Obama administration and urged Russia not to escalate the situation. Flynn later pled guilty to lying to the FBI about these contacts.  Roger Stone (Longtime Trump Advisor) Contact: Communicated with Guccifer 2.0 (a persona operated by Russian military intelligence/GRU) and acted as a liaison regarding WikiLeaks releases. Details: Stone attempted to obtain advance notice regarding WikiLeaks’ releases of hacked Democratic National Committee (DNC) and John Podesta emails.  Carter Page (Foreign Policy Advisor) Contact: Traveled to Moscow in July 2016 to deliver a speech at the New Economic School. Details: Met with high-level Russian figures, including Russian Deputy Prime Minister Arkady Dvorkovich and Russian oil executive Andrey Rozhov.  Michael Cohen (Trump’s Personal Attorney) Contact: Pursued the Trump Tower Moscow project well into the 2016 primary election. Details: Communicated directly with the office of Dmitry Peskov, Vladimir Putin's press secretary, to secure approval and land for the deal. Cohen later pled guilty to lying to Congress about the project's timeline.  Felix Sater (Business Associate) Contact: Worked with Cohen on the Trump Tower Moscow deal. Details: Sater famously emailed Cohen in November 2015, writing: "Our boy can become president of the USA and we can engineer it... I will get all of Putins team on it, I will manage this process."  2. Summary Conclusions of Official Reports  The Mueller Report (2019): Concluded that the Russian government interfered in the 2016 election in a "sweeping and systematic fashion". It established numerous connections between Trump campaign officials and individuals linked to the Russian government. However, investigators did not establish that campaign members engaged in a criminal conspiracy or explicitly coordinated with Russia in its interference operations.  The Senate Intelligence Committee Report (2020): A bipartisan, 1,000-page report that largely affirmed Mueller’s factual findings while providing deeper counterintelligence assessments. It concluded that the Trump campaign was vulnerable to foreign influence operations and highlighted Manafort’s connection to Russian intelligence as a critical vulnerability.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE BRIEFING Pipe Bombs and Synagogue Threat Case, Ogden, Utah Friday, October 23, 2026 UNCLASSIFIED // OPEN SOURCE  BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT A federal grand jury in Salt Lake City has indicted Skyler AJ Rose, 22, of Ogden, Utah. Prosecutors say he posted online threats to blow up a synagogue and kill Jews, and that investigators found six working pipe bombs where he lived. The indictment was returned Oct. 21, and his first federal court appearance was set for today. These are allegations. He is presumed innocent.  WHAT HAPPENED - On Dec. 23, 2025, Rose allegedly posted a string of threats on social media, including "I wanna blow up a synagogue." - The FBI traced the posts to the home where he lived. - Searches allegedly found six pipe bombs, one inert device, materials to build more, and two AK-47-type rifles with ammunition. - Prosecutors say his phone showed he had searched online for a synagogue near him in November 2025, a month before the threats.  THE ACCUSED - Skyler AJ Rose, 22, of Ogden. - Federal charges: possessing an unregistered destructive device, threatening to kill people and destroy a building with explosives, a hate crime count, and child sexual abuse material offenses. - The synagogue has not been publicly named.  CURRENT STATUS - He was first arrested in 2025. The federal indictment followed this week. - The FBI and Ogden police led the case, with help from area bomb squads and the ATF. - No one was hurt.  WHY IT MATTERS FOR FAITH COMMUNITIES This case is close to home for Idaho and the Intermountain West. It follows a pattern safety teams see again and again: hateful posts online, a search for a nearby house of worship, and real weapons at home. The warning signs showed up online first, and someone acted on them.  WHAT YOUR SAFETY TEAM CAN DO 1. Treat online threats against any house of worship as real, and report them to the FBI right away. 2. Teach staff and members what to report: threats, talk of attacks, and unusual interest in your building or schedule. 3. Build a working relationship with local police and your FBI field office before you need it. 4. Know what a suspicious package looks like, and have a plan to clear the building and call 911.  Please pray for the Jewish community in Ogden, and give thanks that this was stopped before anyone was hurt.  Details may change as the case moves through court.

If we’re talking about wizards who could genuinely challenge Voldemort, we need to separate raw magical power from duelling ability, intelligence, and specialised magic.  Albus Dumbledore is the clearest answer. Voldemort himself feared Dumbledore, avoided confronting him directly for years, and recognised him as a serious threat. Their duel at the Ministry in Order of the Phoenix showed that Dumbledore could match Voldemort without fighting to kill him.  Gellert Grindelwald belongs in this conversation, too. He was one of the most powerful Dark wizards in history, and Dumbledore considered defeating him a defining event in his own life. However, Grindelwald’s defeat doesn’t establish that he was equal to Voldemort in every aspect of magical combat.  Severus Snape was exceptionally skilled in Occlumency, Legilimency, potion-making, and advanced defensive magic. His ability to deceive Voldemort for years is extraordinary, but that doesn’t prove he could defeat Voldemort in a straight duel.  Minerva McGonagall was formidable enough to confront Voldemort alongside Kingsley Shacklebolt and Horace Slughorn. However, she was fighting alongside two other accomplished wizards, so that encounter doesn’t establish that she could match him alone.  Bellatrix Lestrange was arguably Voldemort’s most dangerous and trusted duellist among his followers. She defeated experienced opponents and killed Sirius Black, but her loyalty to Voldemort shouldn’t be confused with being close to his overall magical power.  And there’s one important distinction: being the second-most powerful wizard doesn’t automatically make someone the second-most likely to defeat Voldemort. Dumbledore had exceptional magical ability, but Snape’s intelligence and deception made him dangerous in a completely different way.  Ultimately, Dumbledore is the only character whose ability to match Voldemort directly is demonstrated so clearly in the books. Grindelwald is a serious historical contender, while the others have impressive abilities without enough evidence to place them on Voldemort’s level. #HarryPotter

Insurrection Barbie’s comparison of Tucker Carlson to Father Coughlin is a remarkable exercise in guilt by association masquerading as historical scholarship.  Interviewing Aleksandr Dugin becomes an endorsement of Russian authoritarianism. Questioning Israeli intelligence becomes antisemitism. Scrutinizing Miriam Adelson’s political influence becomes an attack on Jewish Americans’ rights. Criticizing liberalism becomes a threat to constitutional government.  None of those conclusions follows automatically from the evidence.  The most revealing maneuver is her treatment of Carlson’s rejection of collective Jewish guilt. Rather than consider it evidence against her thesis, she suggests it’s a strategy of concealment.  So Carlson’s statements count against him, and his denials count against him too. What could possibly disprove an accusation constructed that way?  Father Coughlin openly promoted antisemitic conspiracy theories. Invoking his history does not establish that Carlson shares his ideology.  If Carlson makes a false claim, quote it and disprove it. If he advocates discrimination, demonstrate it. But interviewing controversial figures, challenging Christian Zionism, criticizing powerful Jewish donors, or investigating Israeli foreign influence does not establish hatred of Jews.  The author claims to have examined fifty transcripts, yet offers no reproducible methodology or systematic treatment of contradictory evidence.  Her conclusion was apparently settled before the investigation began.  Historical parallels are not proof. Political disagreement is not antisemitism.  And insinuation is not investigative journalism.

Google’s Threat Intelligence Group found a malware called PROMPTFLUX that could ask Gemini to rewrite its own code every hour.  Why would a malware need to do that? To make itself harder to recognize.   Google officially declared it the first use of JIT AI models in malware development.  services.google.com/fh/files…  What are JIT models?  A just in time is a mini model that’s deployed into an environment to receive tasks, determines what it needs, acquires the necessary capabilities from external sources or a more general model and executes it all live.  It also watches the outcome and continues thinking, changing till it can meet its goal.   Antivirus tools can usually look for patterns in malicious code but if that code keeps changing, it becomes a much for difficult task for the antivirus program and that’s what PROMPTFLUX was designed to do.   Does that make it invincible?  Not entirely. Even an AI malware able to change its code to modify itself cannot just easily walk through a properly set up defense.   Systems no longer just analyze programs at face/code value, they now monitor programs in real time while they run. They also take other heuristic measures and the good ones are able to spot suspicious behaviors when they start and put an end to it even in a trusted program.

<최근 디지털애셋 웹사이트에 발생한 공격에 대해 설명드립니다> 디지털애셋은 지난 10월 20일 오전 9시 30분 해커가 디지털애셋 웹사이트 관리자 계정 인증서를 탈취한 사실을 파악하고 추가 피해 방지를 위해 같은 날 10월 20일 오전 9시 45분부터 10월 21일 오후 1시까지 웹사이트를 폐쇄했습니다.  10월 20일 텔레그램 채널 등에 공지한 것처럼 디지털애셋은 독자들의 회원가입을 받은 적이 없어 개인정보 유출은 일어나지 않았습니다. 다만 관리자 계정 인증서가 탈취되면 기사 무단 게재·삭제·수정 등이 가능해지고 웹페이지 악성코드 삽입 등이 가능해져 이를 방지하기 위해 웹사이트를 일시적으로 닫았습니다.  디지털애셋이 이번에 받은 웹사이트 공격은 크게 2가지로 나눌 수 있을 것 같습니다.  첫째, 디지털애셋 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 대상으로 한 로그인 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 10월 19일 게재된 기사 및 칼럼에서 개발자 도구를 열면 볼 수 있는 정보를 통해 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 파악했습니다. 해커는 파악한 아이디를 기반으로 로그인을 지속적으로 시도했고 이 가운데 관리자가 임의로 설정한 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 뚫었습니다. 이 패스워드는 비밀번호 8자리와 특수문자 1자리로 이뤄졌습니다. 본지 웹페이지를 관리하는 외주 업체는 별도 세션 탈취 없이 이 정도 길이의 패스워드가 뚫린 건 전체 클라이언트 중에서 처음 있는 일이라고 설명했습니다. 해커의 공격 문자열에 오픈소스 AI 침투 도구 ARTEX가 지속적으로 포함돼 AI를 활용한 공격임을 추정할 수 있습니다. 이에 본지는 10월 19일 관리자 페이지에 OTP를 도입하고 뚫린 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 변경했습니다.  둘째, 해커의 관리자 계정 인증서 탈취 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 로그인 공격 시도를 24시간 계속하면서 비회원도 업로드할 수 있는 제보 기능 등을 이용해 악성코드가 심어진 글을 관리자 페이지에 게재했습니다. 이날 관리자 중 2명이 관련 글을 클릭해 해커가 세션 탈취에 성공한 것으로 저희는 보고 있습니다. 해커는 탈취한 인증서를 통해 관리자 권한을 우회 획득했고 웹페이지 배너에 악성코드를 심으려는 시도를 했습니다. 이를 파악한 본지는 웹페이지를 일시 중단하고 종합 보완 조치를 한 후에 10월 21일 웹사이트 운영을 재개했습니다.  AI의 발전으로 불특정다수의 웹사이트에 동시다발적으로 공격을 시도하는 게 가능해지면서 보안 중요도가 상대적으로 낮다는 평가를 받던 비금융 중소기업들의 피해 사례가 늘고 있는 이유를 이번에 체감하게 됐습니다. 또 매체의 경우 신속하고 정확한 기사 게재를 위해 복잡한 로그인 절차 도입이 망설여질 수밖에 없습니다. 그러나 이번 일을 겪으면서 기존 콘텐츠 자산 보호 및 기사 무단 게재 방지를 최우선으로 삼고 복잡한 인증 절차를 도입해야 한다는 걸 절감했습니다. 보안 환경이 하루가 다르게 급변하고 있는데 모두 각자의 정보와 자산을 안전하게 지키시기를 바라는 마음에서 피해 사례를 간략히 공유드렸습니다.

Refrigeration management systems across 700+ French 🇫🇷 supermarkets were compromised in October 2026, with attackers manipulating temperature and defrost controls to cause food losses at scale.  Key findings:  - The confirmed affected systems were Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland and Dixell XWEB. This is not a new threat: pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) claimed over 20 refrigeration attacks since January 2026, mostly targeting fruit storage, wineries, and food processors across Spain 🇪🇸, Italy 🇮🇹, and other European countries. On April 26 alone, Z-Pentest claimed 10 separate hits. The attack method in each case was the same: changing temperature and defrost settings via exposed HMIs, using legitimate supervisory functions.  - Forescout's global exposure scan found 12,976 service observations across 6,017 distinct public IPs in 99 countries. The two attack paths are weak or absent authentication (only 287 of 513 pCOWeb services returned HTTP 401 responses) and known unpatched vulnerabilities. Danfoss AK-SM 800 is end-of-life since May 2021 with no patch path. For AK-SM 800A, 80% of exposed StoreView services run firmware older than 4.3.1, leaving them exposed to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Copeland XWEB Pro has 23 known vulnerabilities below firmware 1.13. CAREL products carry 11 known vulnerabilities across boss, boss mini, and pCOWeb.  - Initial access methods and responsible actors in the French 🇫🇷 incidents remain unconfirmed. Manufacturer documentation for both Danfoss AK-SM and Copeland XWEB explicitly supported direct internet exposure, port forwarding, and HTTP access for remote maintenance, meaning many installations are intentionally reachable. This creates a fractured ownership model: contractors manage the refrigeration platform, facilities teams own hardware, IT manages the network path, and no single party sees the full picture.  - Beyond setpoints, devices like CAREL pCOWeb and XWEB Pro expose Modbus-readable and writable variables, widening the impact potential. Rapid successive configuration changes observed in France 🇫🇷 suggest automation, meaning attackers scripted supervisory API calls rather than making manual adjustments, and those changes can blend into routine contractor activity with no obvious alert.  For responders and operators: the audit gap here is the correlation problem. A supervisory session log may not record which setpoint changed; a controller alarm may not identify the account behind it. Hunting for this activity means correlating remote-access session timestamps against defrost schedule changes, temperature setpoint modifications, alarm suppressions, and user account changes in the controller audit log. Review NAT and port-forwarding rules for port 80 and 443 terminating at refrigeration management interfaces. Prioritize replacing Danfoss AK-SM 800 (no patch exists) and patching AK-SM 800A to firmware 4.3.1 or later. The Forescout report details the full vulnerability table by product family.  #DFIR_Radar

⚠️ Unexpected login prompt in Outlook Web: what a researcher observed, and why it matters  Security researcher Jesus A. (algo.help) shared an unusual observation with us.  While reading a newsletter email in Outlook Web, a browser-native "Sign in" dialog suddenly appeared, asking for a username and password. He hadn't clicked anything or opened a login page.  🔍 What he found In the browser's DevTools, an image embedded in the email was being loaded from a third-party marketing server. That request returned HTTP 401 Unauthorized, with outlook.live.com as the referrer. A 401 is how a web server says "credentials required." When it comes with an authentication challenge, the browser itself can draw a login box.  In other words, simply opening an email may have caused a server outside Microsoft to ask the reader for credentials.  🎣 Why this matters This is an old but effective phishing idea. Fake login pages are getting easier to spot, but a native browser dialog: • Has no logos, branding or bad design to give it away • Looks like it comes from the browser or the app you're using • Appears while you're inside a trusted service like Outlook  A user who types their Microsoft password into that box sends it to whoever runs the remote server, not to Microsoft.  📌 Status: unconfirmed To be clear about what is and isn't known: • Observed once, on Sept 12, 2026 (Brave, Chromium 152) • No longer reproducible. The resource now returns 404 • The server's WWW-Authenticate header wasn't captured, so the exact cause can't be confirmed • The 401 may have had a harmless cause, such as an expired campaign asset or a misconfiguration • There is no evidence of malicious intent by the newsletter sender or its email platform • Reported to Microsoft (MSRC) on Oct 15. Receipt acknowledged, no technical assessment yet  🛡️ What you should do • Never enter credentials into a pop-up that appears while reading email • Check which domain is asking. Microsoft sign-ins happen at login.microsoftonline.com or login.live.com, not in a bare browser dialog • Consider blocking external images by default in your email client • Admins: watch for remote content in inbound mail that returns 401 challenges  We'll update if Microsoft responds.  Full technical write-up by Jesus A. 👇 algo.help/outlook-authentica… #CyberSecurity #Phishing #Outlook #InfoSec

sample_tweets.text: I want to caveat this since based on some comments, people are interpreting it in a way other than was intended. You 10000% need to update your PHP version. php2shell is no joke.  I am NOT saying people don't have functional exploits...they do. I'm saying that most of the public ones are AI hallucinations, and there's also some complexities which lower the risk of something apocalyptic, like a self-propagating worm that blasts through the entire internet (À la. EnternalBlue or Log4J).  The chances are if you used some click-to-deploy container, installed your web stack from a tutorial, or copy and pasted a command from somewhere, you're probably running the same exact config as a gazillion other people. There is no guarantee someone won't publicly release an exploit that affects you setup, or multiple major setups. There is no way for you to know ahead of time.  Additionally, if you're running mod_php, that appears to be the easiest target of all. php-fpm and other configs are not immune, I've seen working exploits for all. But mod_php is the easiest, so I'd recommend not only updating PHP, but planning to migrate to something newer, like PHP-FPM.  I would bet good money this is not the last of the critical PHP bugs we're going to see, and the next ones could be easier to exploit. In which case you get less time to update.   Updating your PHP version is the absoloute bare minimum you NEED to do. Harden your servers, install security monitoring/detection tools, and please, please, migrate off mod_php if you can, it's obsolete af.

This is 100% correct when looking at it from a single-system perspective. ASLR does not create a significant barrier to successful exploitation. But when looking at it from a mass-exploitation perspective, there are a lot of hidden complexities that come into play.  Vulnerability research is one of the few fields where you tend to make more money on the right side of the law. There isn't a huge demand for black market exploits. Most of the money is in bug bounty, working as a vulnerability researcher, or selling to grey-market exploit brokers.  This means that even the smallest bit of added complexity can take a vulnerability from 'cybercriminal free-for-all' to 'unlikely to be widely exploited'.   Mass-exploitation events are almost always preceded by someone publishing fully-weaponized point-and-click exploit code. It's extremely rare for criminal groups to successfully develop exploit for higher-complexity vulnerabilities on their own, even with AI.  So, less researchers capable of exploiting the bug means less chance of a working weaponized exploit being posted online. But also, the increased difficulty of exploitation, thus increased time/effort, discourages those who can exploit the bug from giving it away for free.  There's also per-target variability (which I don't know for sure is the case with this bug). But with more complex bugs, it'll sometimes be impossible to make universal exploits. In extreme cases, attackers may need to build exploit for each specific system or software version, or each specific config, or maybe even both.  So, while it's correct that it's not hard to find an ASLR bypass, it is difficult to find a bypass that works reliably at scale. So far, most of the working exploits I've seen are limited to just a handful of PHP versions, or bruteforcing ASLR. And that makes all the difference when it comes to the risk of threat actors spraying exploits at the entire internet.  For this specific exploit, the honest answer is, I don't know. It's above my pay grade. But I'm almost 100% certain that the level of bad this will be will be directly dependent on what kind of exploits security researchers make public.

Look, compromises happen to everyone. I have received a ton of private messages asking if I'm okay. But the reality is that I stopped using Windoze a long time ago and this was a kind of one-off thing where I was trying to re-image an old system anyway (away from Windoze).

A kind reader submitted the Rufus installer to any.run, a sandbox which walks through the installation of software to find malware that gets installed only *AFTER* the executable is clicked. You can see exactly all of the post-install prompts to download additional software that I also saw. https:// infosec.exchange/@jordinki/117 492425049116266
However, in my defense Google's default search results list rufus[.]ie as the authoritative site

No clue whether the resulting ISO is also malicious, but tried running it just for giggles on a spare Windows PC from bootup and the machine's bios said nope, wouldn't allow b/c security policy. Not sure if it's related but I've never seen that message before trying to boot up from a USB.

Not sure who needs to know this, but if you download and install the Windows version of Rufus, the free software for writing ISO images to USB/CD-ROM, your PC will end up with about 100 trojans. Edit: The site I downloaded from was rufus[.]ie which is apparently the official site. During installation, the software threw up a couple of rather verbose messages saying it needed to download additional components.

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협 환경은 PHP 및 Node.js와 같은 핵심 런타임 환경의 RCE 취약점(PHP2Shell, Node2Shell)을 악용하는 공격이 급증하며 전 세계 웹 인프라에 심각한 위협을 가하고 있습니다 ([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/ruby-fixes-three-regex-engine-bugs.html)). 특히 공격자들은 AI 에이전트를 활용하여 침투 과정을 자동화하고, 대규모 환경에서 취약점을 스캔하거나 인증 정보를 탈취하는 등 공격 효율성을 극대화하고 있습니다 ([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/cybersecurity-operations/ai-tools-massive-attacks-little-cost)). 또한, UEFI Bootkit인 BlackX와 같이 OS 이전 단계에서 보안 부팅을 우회하는 고도화된 공격 기법이 외교 및 국가 기관을 대상으로 지속적으로 관찰되고 있습니다 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **APT41**: [Securelist](https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/) - 중앙아시아 외교 기관을 타겟으로 BlackX UEFI Bootkit을 배포하여 보안 부팅 우회 및 지속성 확보.
- **Lazarus**: [Securelist](https://securelist.com/lazarus-operation-flashhole/121541/) - Operation FlashHole 캠페인을 통해 금융 보안 소프트웨어(CrossWeb EX)를 악용하고 워터링 홀 기법으로 공격 수행.
- **Storm-0940**: [Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/tag-217-artex-south-korean-banks) - AI 프레임워크 ARTEX를 활용하여 Microsoft 365 클라우드 테넌트 2,250개를 자동화된 방식으로 침해.
- **n0n**: [데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209036) - 한진정보통신을 해킹하여 고객사 계정 정보 및 인력 배치 현황 등 민감 데이터 탈취 및 유출.

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **한진정보통신 해킹**: 랜섬웨어 조직 'n0n'에 의해 한진정보통신이 해킹되어 개인정보 및 공급망 관련 데이터가 유출됨 ([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209036)).
- **북한 연계 조직의 PHP2Shell 공격 정황**: 한국 정부 및 금융기관을 대상으로 PHP2Shell 취약점을 악용하려는 시도가 포착됨 ([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209035)).
- **TAG-217의 금융권 공격**: ARTEX AI 도구를 사용하여 국내 금융기관을 타겟으로 한 공격 사례 확인 ([Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/tag-217-artex-south-korean-banks)).

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
- **CVE-2026-109618 / 109619**: PHP RCE (PHP2Shell), CVSS 9.2, 전 세계 웹 서버 대상 악용 중 ([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/))

- **CVE-2022-21894**: Baton Drop (BlackX Bootkit 악용), UEFI 보안 부팅 우회 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/))
